Agentsensus: Consensus-Compressed Shared Memory for
Multi-Agent Story-World Simulation

A shared long-term memory that merges agents’ equivalent memories into multi-witness records and self-organizes into a navigable memory graph.

Scenarios Three Kingdoms (三国演义) (80 rounds, 33 active agents) · Russia–Ukraine (40 rounds, 47 active) · Red Chamber (红楼梦) (80 rounds, 34 active) · Hamlet (40 rounds, 16 active) Checkpointing every 20 rounds Model gpt-5-mini
Abstract

Multi-agent story-world simulations give every character a private memory stream, so one shared event is stored once per witness, its copies drift apart as agents paraphrase and summarize them, and nothing links a courier’s report to the battle it describes. We present Agentsensus, a story-world simulation framework whose long-term memory is a single store in which sharing is computed rather than assumed. Each deposit is atomized into self-contained statements; a statement close to an existing one is put to an LLM equivalence judge and, if the two are equivalent, merged into one record whose owner set is the union of its witnesses. Statements split from one deposit are cross-linked, and recall expands one hop along those links. Ownership stays scoped — an agent recalls only what it owns — so compression never leaks knowledge between characters, and every mechanism runs inside remember and recall, the only two memory operations agents demonstrably use: across two models and four backends, discretionary memory management was invoked zero times. Across four worlds — two classical Chinese novels, Hamlet, and a real-world conflict timeline — run for 40 to 80 rounds against three per-agent memory baselines under an equal-granularity protocol, consensus writes 22–44% fewer entries than the closest baseline and is the only backend whose memories become shared (14–28% multi-owner, single records reaching 10 witnesses) and linked (94–99%), at judged continuation quality indistinguishable from the baselines. The memory substrate alone recovers the story’s social organization: agents who converse overlap in memory 23× more than those who do not, and cross-agent memory links run almost exclusively between conversing pairs.

1 Introduction

A story-world simulation places dozens of LLM-driven characters in a world with places, objects and documents, and lets a narrative emerge from what they say and do to one another [1, 2]. Unlike a task-solving multi-agent system, where the team is judged on an answer it produces [10, 12, 13], such a world is judged on what it accumulates: who learned what, when, and from whom. Memory is therefore not a component of these systems but their substrate. It is also the component that scales worst. A novel-seeded world starts with thousands of canonical events already deposited, adds several hundred more per hundred rounds of simulation, and must serve retrieval to every character at every round.

The dominant memory design, established by Generative Agents [1] and inherited by most subsequent frameworks [2, 8], gives each character a private, append-only stream scored by recency, importance and relevance. This is faithful to individual cognition — people do remember separately — but as the substrate of a shared world it creates three structural problems, each of which worsens as the world grows:

  • P1 — Witness-multiplied redundancy. Every shared experience is stored once per participant: a war council attended by ten officers produces ten near-identical records, and a novel-seeded world multiplies this by thousands of canonical events. Storage, embedding cost and retrieval-index size scale with the number of witnesses rather than the number of events — in our four testbeds the per-agent baselines carry 28–79% more entries than the consensus store for the same history.
  • P2 — Fragmented, divergence-prone world knowledge. The same event exists as N independently-worded copies that drift further apart as agents paraphrase, summarize and reflect on them. No mechanism reconciles them, no record knows its counterparts exist, and nothing connects a courier’s report to the battle it describes or the order it triggers. The connective tissue of the story exists nowhere in the memory substrate — only implicitly in the transcript — so retrieval returns one agent’s partial, possibly stale view even when the collective already holds the full picture.
  • P3 — Memory management that agents never perform. Stream designs expose maintenance operations — linking related records, revising stale ones, forgetting duplicates — and implicitly rely on agents to use them. Empirically they do not: across two models and all four backends we test, agents issued zero calls to every discretionary memory-management action, even with documentation, worked examples and an id-free interface (§5.6). An architecture that depends on agent-side curation therefore never acquires structure in practice, however well the operations are designed.

Our approach. Agentsensus answers all three with one architectural commitment: the world’s memory is a single store, and sharing is computed, not assumed. Memories stay owner-scoped — an agent recalls only what it owns, so a shared store is not a shared mind — but when two agents record the same event, an equivalence mechanism detects it and folds the records into one entry owned by both. This is deduplication with a semantic rather than lexical criterion, closer to record linkage [24] and semantic corpus deduplication [26] than to caching, and it addresses P1 together with the divergence half of P2. Pieces split from one compound deposit are automatically cross-linked, and recall expands one hop along those links into what the caller also owns, giving the store the connective tissue P2 demands without an agent ever building a graph. And because of P3, every mechanism runs inside remember and recall themselves — the two operations agents demonstrably do use — rather than being offered as curation the agents would have to remember to perform.

What we find. We evaluate on four worlds chosen to differ in what a memory must hold: two classical Chinese novels (Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Dream of the Red Chamber), one English play (Hamlet), and one real-world conflict timeline (Russia–Ukraine) whose actors are institutions rather than people. Each runs 40–80 rounds against three faithful baseline reimplementations under an equal-granularity protocol that routes every backend’s writes through the same atomizer, so entry counts are comparable and only the mechanism differs. Three findings hold across all four worlds. Structure is exclusive to consensus: it is the only backend whose memories become multi-owner (14–28%) or linked (94–99%); the baselines sit at exactly zero on both, by construction rather than by tuning. Compression compounds with horizon: sharing rises monotonically as a run is extended — 13%→20%→23%→24% in Red Chamber at rounds 10/40/60/80 — because later deposits meet a store that already holds their equivalents. The graph is meaningful, not incidental: agents who converse overlap in memory 23× more than agents who do not, and cross-agent memory links run almost exclusively between conversing pairs, so the social structure of the story can be read off the memory substrate alone.

Two findings are negative and we report them as such. Judged continuation quality does not separate the backends: over four worlds and four metrics, consensus leads four of sixteen cells and trails elsewhere by margins the size of the scoring noise (§5.3). And goal-pursuit consistency saturates at 0.96–0.99 for every backend, because the agent loop keeps a goal on the stack almost always — a metric that certifies the loop rather than discriminating between memories. The case for consensus compression is that it buys structure and footprint at no measurable cost in behaviour, not that it writes better stories.

Contributions.

  • A story-world simulation framework with a deterministic round-barrier scheduler, passive environments and information carriers, kernel-held conversation threads with distance-delayed delivery, and full-system checkpoints enabling bit-for-bit resumption.
  • A consensus-compressed shared memory: self-contained atomization, semantic-prefilter plus LLM-judged equivalence merging with owner-set union, automatic affiliation of split pieces, and auto-expanding owner-scoped recall — all of it inside the two operations agents actually call.
  • An equal-granularity, simulation-only evaluation protocol against three faithful baseline reimplementations, isolating the memory mechanism from confounds of storage granularity and seeded content, applied to four worlds spanning two languages, three genres and both human and institutional actors.
  • A three-layer case-study methodology (interaction graph, memory-affiliation graph, ownership relation) quantifying how the emergent memory structure tracks the story’s social structure.
  • Two negative results that constrain how such systems should be designed and evaluated: agents never perform discretionary memory management, so structure must be mechanized; and judged narrative quality is insensitive to the memory architecture at this scale, so memory designs should be argued on structure and cost rather than on quality scores.

2 Related Work

2.1  Memory for a single LLM agent

Generative Agents [1] established the design most agent systems still use: a per-agent stream of observations scored by recency, importance and relevance, periodically compressed into reflections. Variants change what is stored or how it is maintained rather than who owns it. MemGPT [4] treats context as an operating-system memory hierarchy that the model itself pages in and out; MemoryBank [16] adds a forgetting curve so old memories decay; Reflexion [5] persists verbal self-feedback across episodes; Voyager [17] accumulates reusable skills rather than episodes. A-MEM [7] is closest to our linking mechanism: it connects an agent’s notes into an evolving network as they are written. A survey of the area [8] finds the same shape throughout — the memory belongs to one agent, and structure, where it exists, is built inside that agent’s own store. Agentsensus keeps the atomization and retrieval machinery of this line but makes ownership a property of a record rather than of a store, which is what allows one record to belong to several agents at once.

2.2  Multi-agent systems and their shared state

Multi-agent frameworks organize LLMs into teams: AutoGen [10] around conversable agents, CAMEL [11] around role-played dialogue, MetaGPT [12] and ChatDev [13] around a software-engineering process with defined roles. In all of them the shared state is the conversation — a transcript or blackboard the agents read — and long-term memory, where present, remains per-agent. This is adequate when a team works a task to completion, but a story world runs for hundreds of rounds and no transcript survives as a retrieval substrate at that length. Our kernel keeps conversation threads (so a message has a place and a delay) but treats them as transport, not as memory.

2.3  Memory shared across agents

Two systems address the multi-agent case directly. G-Memory [3] organizes a system’s history into a three-tier insight/query/interaction hierarchy, queried at both team and agent level, and is our G-Memory baseline. Collaborative Memory [9] shares fragments between users under a dynamic access-control policy that decides who may read what, and is our collaborative baseline. Both keep every contributor’s record intact and mediate access to those records; neither merges records that say the same thing across contributors. That difference is the subject of this paper: consensus compression changes the number of records rather than the visibility of them, and the owner set it produces is the access-control policy, derived rather than configured.

2.4  Deduplication, record linkage and grounding

The idea that two descriptions may denote one fact is older than LLM agents. Record linkage [24] formalized deciding whether two records refer to the same entity; semantic deduplication of web-scale corpora [26] showed that embedding-space near-duplicates can be removed without loss, which is the pre-filter half of our merge. What our setting adds is that the duplicate carries a witness: merging is not only a saving but a statement that two characters share a belief, which is why the merged record keeps a set of owners rather than a single canonical author. The psycholinguistic notion of grounding — the mutual knowledge interlocutors build and rely on [25] — is the phenomenon our owner sets approximate mechanically.

2.5  Retrieval and graph-structured knowledge

Retrieval-augmented generation [14] is the standard way to give a model access to more than fits in context, and graph-structured variants improve multi-hop and global questions: HippoRAG [6] indexes a corpus as an entity graph, GraphRAG [15] builds an entity graph and community summaries for query-focused summarization. These build structure over a static corpus, in an indexing pass with global knowledge of the documents. Our graph is built incrementally at deposit time by agents who cannot see the store, from two signals available locally: which atoms came from one deposit, and which existing record an incoming atom was judged equivalent to.

2.6  Story worlds, character agents and social simulation

Story generation with language models has largely been a planning problem: Dramatron [19] generates scripts hierarchically from a logline, Re3 [20] and DOC [21] plan and revise long stories against an outline. Character agents come at fiction from the other side, fitting a model to one persona [18]. Between them sit simulated worlds: the Smallville society of Generative Agents [1], scaled-up interview-grounded populations [22], geopolitical simulations whose agents are states [23], and BookWorld [2], which builds an interactive agent society from a novel and extracts per-character memories from the source — the same motivation as our sedimentation stage. Agentsensus differs from all of these in what it puts under test: not the story that comes out, but the memory substrate it comes from, measured by footprint, sharing, graph structure and their growth with horizon. The story is still evaluated (§5.3), but as a check that compression costs nothing, not as the claim.

3 The Agentsensus Framework

3.1  Design motivation

The per-agent memory stream is the default because it is the obvious model of a mind: what an agent knows is what it saw. In a shared world, however, that model makes three structural commitments that the designer never explicitly chose, and each one compounds with the number of agents and the length of the run.

Storage scales with witnesses, not with events. A council attended by ten officers is ten records. Nothing in the system can tell that they describe one event, so embedding cost, index size, and retrieval noise all grow with the cast rather than with the story. Seeding a world from a novel multiplies the effect before round 0: on the same sedimented chapters the per-agent baselines carry 3.3–5.7× the entries of a merged store (§5.1).

Nothing reconciles the copies, and nothing connects them. The ten records are ten independently-worded paraphrases that only diverge further as agents summarize and reflect. No record knows its counterparts exist; no edge links a courier’s report to the battle it describes or to the order it triggered. The connective tissue of the story lives in the transcript, not in the memory, so retrieval returns one agent’s partial view even when the collective already holds the whole.

The interfaces that could fix this go unused. Stream designs expose maintenance operations — link related records, revise stale ones, forget duplicates — and rely on agents to call them. Across two models and all four backends we measure zero such calls (§5.6), with documentation, worked examples, and an id-free interface all in place. Any structure that depends on agent-side curation therefore never materializes.

Agentsensus answers all three with one commitment: the world’s memory is a single store, and sharing is computed rather than assumed. Three design decisions follow, and the rest of this section is their mechanics. D1 — equivalence merging: when two agents record the same event, the write path detects it and folds the records into one row whose owner-set is the union of its witnesses, so cost tracks events. D2 — deposit-time graph: the atoms split from one deposit are linked to each other as a side effect of writing, so the graph exists without anyone maintaining it. D3 — structure inside remember/recall: because agents demonstrably use only those two operations, every mechanism lives inside them; nothing is delegated to agent discretion.

Figure 1 shows the framework these decisions live in; Figure 2 shows what they change inside the store.

3.2  System overview

Agentsensus is three subsystems, all visible in Figure 1. An offline sedimentation pipeline turns a source text into a memory-grounded initial world. A deterministic round-barrier kernel schedules agents, routes messages, and snapshots the entire system. The shared long-term memory holds every agent’s knowledge in one store, with D1–D3 implemented inside its write and read paths. Data flows left to right at start-up — sedimentation seeds both the store and the world state — and cycles between kernel and store at run time: Phase-2 action effects write into the store and into conversation threads, and both feed the next round’s agent views through owner-scoped recall and the conversation roster.

3.3  World model and round-barrier kernel

Entities. A world is a set of agents on a location map with pairwise travel distances. Characters are LLM-driven: each holds a persona, a goal stack, a status register, and a short-term FIFO of recent actions; each decision is one LLM call that receives a rendered view (round, goals, status, FIFO, co-located agents, conversation roster, known locations, plus contextual hints) and returns one action as JSON. Environments and information carriers are passive: they own memories (deposited by sedimentation or by characters’ act_on) but never take turns — a character’s act_on/read is served synchronously by the kernel against the target’s own memories, costing no extra LLM calls and giving places and documents durable, queryable state.

Scheduling. Each round runs two phases under a barrier. Phase 1 builds every awake character’s view from the same pre-round snapshot and issues all decisions concurrently; because views are frozen before any decision, LLM latency cannot change what any agent observes. Phase 2 applies the returned actions sequentially in a fixed agent order, so conflicting effects resolve deterministically and event order is reproducible independent of API timing. Agents sleep only by explicit wait; a single sleep is capped (20 rounds) after we observed uncapped waits produce narrative deadlocks — a character who delegated a task and slept “until the report arrives” was simply never messaged again and stayed silent for 52 rounds. A wake=true message still interrupts sleep early.

Messaging. Messages are not agent-held inboxes but kernel-held conversation threads, one per interlocutor pair. Co-located speech delivers at the next round; remote messages travel for their map distance in rounds, so information propagates at the speed of couriers rather than instantaneously. Delivery increments the recipient’s unread counter (surfaced in its view roster) and, by default, wakes it; reading is an explicit read_thread action. The same threads also log observation and environment interactions, giving each pair a complete interaction history.

Checkpointing. Every 20 rounds the kernel atomically snapshots the complete system — each agent’s short-term state (FIFO, goal stack, status, sleep timer), kernel runtime (presence, in-transit moves, undelivered messages, conversation threads, event counter), and the entire memory store including embeddings. A resumed run continues bit-for-bit; the long-horizon results in §5 are consecutive resumed stages of one continuous run per backend.

3.4  Sedimentation: from source text to memory-grounded world

The pipeline converts the sediment span into the initial world in four steps. (i) Extraction and attribution: an LLM pass extracts events chapter by chapter and attributes each to the characters who witnessed it, producing atomic, story-ordered records with owner-sets. (ii) Per-backend ingest: each memory backend stores these events under its own rule — the consensus store keeps one merged row per event carrying the full owner-set, while per-agent baselines fan out one row per witness — so every method starts from the initial state its own mechanism would have produced, and baseline machinery (importance scoring, reflection, distillation) is run over the sediment before round 0. (iii) Boundary-state finalization: each character’s aliveness and location at the story boundary are extracted from its own memory timeline (with a canon-knowledge fallback anchored to the boundary chapter); characters dead by the boundary are archived — they keep their memories as owners but are never scheduled — and living ones are placed at their last grounded location. (iv) The result is a world whose knowledge and geography are both grounded in the text.

3.5  The consensus shared memory

Data model. The store is a single vector collection whose rows are (text, embedding, owner-set, affiliated-set, metadata). Owner membership is additionally materialized as indexed per-agent flags, so owner-scoped retrieval is a server-side filter rather than a post-hoc scan; the affiliated-set holds ids of related rows and is what makes the store a graph.

Write path. Every remember(text) runs four stages. (1) Atomization: a compound deposit is split by an LLM into atomic statements, each required to be self-contained — pronouns resolved to names, who/what/where carried over — so a statement is interpretable without its siblings. All four backends share this exact stage (§4.3), making entry counts comparable by construction. (2) Candidate pre-filter: each atom is embedded and matched against the store by cosine kNN with a deliberately permissive threshold (0.70): self-contained phrasings of the same event from different viewpoints embed measurably further apart than near-identical wordings, and at the conventional 0.86 zero cross-witness sim memories ever reached candidacy. (3) Equivalence judging: an LLM judge inspects the candidates and either selects the one that describes the same event or declines. The pre-filter only bounds the judge’s candidate list; the judge is the actual gate, so the permissive threshold trades a few extra judge calls for recall of true matches. (4) Merge or insert: on a match the records fold into one row — owner-sets union, affiliated-sets union, the shorter text is kept — so N witnesses of one event cost one row; otherwise a fresh row is inserted. Finally, auto-affiliation mutually links the atoms split from one deposit: the memory graph is built as a side-effect of writing, by the mechanism rather than the agent.

Read path. recall(query) retrieves the top-k semantic matches among rows the caller owns, then follows each hit’s affiliated edges one hop and appends linked rows the caller also owns, marked via_affiliated. A single recall therefore returns an event’s scattered pieces together. Expansion is deliberately uncapped; its cost is measured in §5.2.

Cost placement. The design pays at write time (one atomization call when a deposit is compound, one judge call when candidates pass the pre-filter) to keep the store small and structured; reads add only vector lookups. §5.2’s latency instrumentation quantifies both sides against the baselines.

3.6  How the four designs differ

Everything above is shared by the four backends we compare: the same world model, the same sedimented events, the same two operations, the same atomization. They differ in one place only — the internal structure of the store in Figure 1 — and Figure 2 draws that structure for each. Read side by side, the three baselines differ in how much structure they build within a single owner’s records, and consensus is the only one that builds structure across owners.

3.7  Query-addressed operations and the design rule

No memory operation takes a raw id. forget, revise_memory, and the affiliation operations address a memory by a natural-language query that the kernel resolves to the caller’s best-matching owned row, so owner-scoping is enforced at resolution and there is no id for an agent to mishandle. The design responds to a robust behavioral finding: LLM agents never thread opaque ids across turns — in earlier runs every id-based operation had ≈0 uses. Query addressing removes that interface barrier; the observation that agents still issue zero discretionary memory-management calls (§5.6) is what elevates “structure must live inside remember/recall” from an implementation choice to the framework’s central design rule.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1  Scenarios

Three Kingdoms (三国演义) chapters 1–40 are sedimented onto 191 canonical characters (33 active at the boundary, the rest archived as dead; ~6,000 consensus events). All four backends then run the same 80-round simulation — same scenario file, same action repertoire, same model (gpt-5-mini; embeddings text-embedding-3-small) — in four checkpointed 20-round stages.

To test that the mechanisms are not an artifact of one fictional world, the second scenario is real-world: a timeline of the Russia–Ukraine conflict sedimented through 2026-07 (1,533 events over 170 entities). Real-world boundary semantics replace the novel’s: a figure is archived if, by the boundary, they are dead or out of the conflict’s stage (out of office, dismissed, disbanded), with placements grounded in the timeline or, failing that, the person’s workplace/role (final cast: 47 active, 14 archived, manually verified). All four backends run the same 40-round simulation under the identical fairness protocol.

The third scenario returns to fiction in a different register: Red Chamber (红楼梦) (Dream of the Red Chamber), chapters 1–40 sedimented onto 152 registry characters (6,506 consensus events; chapters 41–80 held out). The active cast is the 37 characters above the memory threshold (34 living; Qin Keqing (秦可卿), Jia Rui (贾瑞) and Qin Zhong (秦钟), dead by chapter 40, stay archived owners), and the boundary state is a freeze-frame of chapter 40’s garden banquet — Grandmother Jia (贾母) and Granny Liu (刘姥姥) at the Grand View Pavilion (大观楼), the touring party at Hengwu Court (蘅芜苑), the musicians at the Lotus Fragrance Pavilion (藕香榭) — grounded per character in the sediment and manually verified. Where Three Kingdoms is war and statecraft among factions, Red Chamber is dense domestic society — one household, fine-grained relationships — a different social topology for the same mechanisms. All four backends run the same 80-round simulation under the identical fairness protocol.

The fourth scenario is deliberately the smallest: Hamlet, Acts 1–3 sedimented onto a 22-character registry (1,135 consensus events; Acts 4–5 held out). Sixteen characters pass the memory threshold, plus Fortinbras, who owns no sediment memories at all — he never appears on stage before Act 4 — but is retained because the continuation is his; England is likewise retained as an environment because it is where the sealed commission leads. Two characters are archived at the boundary: Polonius, killed behind the arras in 3.4, and the Ghost, absent from the canon after that scene. Where the other three worlds have dozens of agents spread over a map, Hamlet is a chamber drama — sixteen agents in one castle, most scenes a two-person exchange — which makes it the sharpest test of whether the mechanisms need scale to show anything. All four backends run the same 40-round simulation under the identical fairness protocol.

4.2  Baselines

  • Generative-Agents memory [1]: per-agent private streams; insert-time importance scoring; reflection synthesis over high-importance windows.
  • G-Memory [3]: shared store organized as interaction/insight tiers with periodic LLM distillation into insight nodes and bi-level retrieval over provenance edges.
  • Collaborative memory [9]: per-owner fragments guarded by access-control lists; recall is ACL-filtered server-side.

All three ingest the sediment under their own rule (one row per witness) and run their own machinery over it (GA importance+reflections; G-Memory distillation) before round 0, so each starts from a self-consistent initial state.

4.3  Fairness protocol

Equal granularity. Every backend routes remember through the same atomization code with the same self-containment requirement. Entry counts are therefore directly comparable; the only remaining difference is what each mechanism does with identical atoms.

Simulation-only accounting. All reported numbers cover memories the simulation itself generated (remember/act_on deposits). Sedimented content and baseline by-products (GA reflection nodes, G-Memory distillation nodes) are excluded on all sides.

4.4  Metrics

  • Structure (deterministic): sim-entry count; share of multi-owner entries; share of entries with affiliated edges.
  • Continuation quality (LLM-judged, mean±std over 3 scorings of the run’s rendered screenplay): grounding — the fraction of the sim’s own events consistent with the canon; trajectory — agreement of character arcs with reference arcs extracted from each world’s held-out continuation (Three Kingdoms: chapters 41–60; Red Chamber: chapters 41–80; Russia–Ukraine: the timeline beyond the 2024-04 boundary; Hamlet: Acts 4–5); narrative — judged coherence/drama/fidelity (1–5); goal pursuit — whether each agent’s actions consistently pursue its declared goals, judged against the goal stack the agent itself maintains and read from the event log rather than the screenplay; achievement is deliberately not scored, since a faithful tragedy requires goals to fail. Scoring reads the screenplay rather than the raw transcript (§5.3): a 40-round Russia–Ukraine log is 1.6M characters, past any judge’s context window, while its screenplay is an order of magnitude smaller and in one language, so no truncation or sampling is needed. Where a held-out span is itself too long to read at once — Red Chamber’s forty chapters — reference arcs are extracted chapter-group by chapter-group and condensed per character.
  • Operation latency (§5.2): per-call wall-clock time of remember/recall, timed in the kernel around the backend call so each mechanism’s internal cost (equivalence judging, importance scoring, auto-expansion) falls inside the window. Rounds 61–80 are instrumented live; rounds 1–60 are measured by replaying each stage’s logged operations against the store state the stage started from (checkpoint-exact for stages 2–3; the first stage’s GA/G-Memory replay stores lack prime by-products, ≈3–5% of rows).
  • Three-layer alignment (§5.4): relations between the interaction graph, the affiliation graph, and the ownership relation.

5 Results

5.1  Footprint and structure

At equal granularity, consensus writes the fewest sim memories in all three worlds (Three Kingdoms: 974 vs 1251–1455; Russia–Ukraine: 814 vs 1091–1268; Red Chamber: 438 vs 785–882) because merging folds witnesses together. The same holds for structure: in every world consensus is the only backend whose memories become shared and linked (19%/97% in Three Kingdoms, 14%/99% in Russia–Ukraine, 24%/94% in Red Chamber), against 0% for every baseline.

Two columns, two effects. The sediment column is consensus compression applied to the seeded history, and its multiplier is a property of the world rather than of the mechanism: the per-witness fan-out is 3.3× in Three Kingdoms, 4.1–5.7× in Red Chamber, 5.5–9.4× in Russia–Ukraine and 4.7–6.2× in Hamlet, tracking the average number of witnesses per event, which a war room with institutional spokespeople maximizes and a two-hander chamber drama minimizes. The sim column is the same effect measured over events the simulation itself generated, at rates of roughly 12 (Three Kingdoms), 20 (Russia–Ukraine), 5 (Red Chamber) and 4 (Hamlet) consensus entries per round. Everything else in §5 is computed over the sim column only.

5.1.1  Three Kingdoms (三国演义)

Discussion. Two readings matter here. First, the footprint gap is mechanistic, not behavioral: all four backends receive the same actions and atomize identically, so the 481-entry spread between consensus and the largest baseline is exactly the number of times the equivalence judge folded one agent’s record into another’s — each fold is a deduplicated witness (P1). Second, the structural columns are all-or-nothing by design: per-agent stores have no cross-agent rows to merge and no deposit-siblings to link, so the 19% / 97% columns measure capabilities the baselines lack architecturally, not parameters they tuned differently.

Merged records are precisely the cross-viewpoint deduplication the mechanism targets — 38 memories carry three or more witnesses (maximum 6):

owners = [hanxiandi, xiahoudun, xiahouyuan, xushu, yuejin, yujin]  “Xiahou Yuan led three hundred light cavalry out of Xuchang on reconnaissance, in three columns.” (夏侯渊率三百轻骑分三路从许昌出城侦察。)
owners = [hanxiandi, xiahoudun, xushu, yujin, zhangliao]  “Yue Jin was put in charge of Xuchang’s grain and military supplies.” (乐进督管许昌的粮草与军需。)
owners = [hanxiandi, xiahoudun, xushu, yuejin, yujin]  “Zhang Liao was appointed overall commander of Xuchang’s defences.” (张辽被任为许昌防务的总摄指挥。)

5.1.2  Russia–Ukraine

Discussion. The same two readings hold at one eighth the horizon: the 19–30% footprint gap is again exactly the number of equivalence-judge folds, and the structural columns remain all-or-nothing — 0% for every per-agent baseline. What is new is the real-world flavor of the folds: equivalence merges a person’s record into their institution’s — the same mechanism that fuses two officers’ views of one battle fuses a spokesperson’s statement with its organization’s record of it.

Merged records again pair one event seen from two sides — characteristically a person and their institution:

owners = [guterres, un]  “António Guterres at UN Headquarters in New York asked the United Nations to assemble a mediation team comprising DPA, OCHA, WFP, UN Political Affairs, and UN Legal to support renewal of the Black Sea grain agreement.”
owners = [podolyak, ukrainian_government]  “Mykhailo Podolyak reported that overnight Russian drone strikes struck Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.”
owners = [kremlin, sobyanin]  “Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin requested authorization to release public instructions to Moscow residents.”

5.1.3  Red Chamber (红楼梦)

Discussion. Red Chamber is where the two claims of §5.1 can be watched separating in time, because it was run at four horizons. Structure was already complete at ten rounds (13% shared, 87% linked, baselines 0%); footprint was not — the four backends then sat at 62–98 entries with consensus not the smallest, within run-to-run variance. From forty rounds on consensus is lowest and stays lowest, and the gap holds as both sides grow: 216 vs 379–492 at forty, 338 vs 625–683 at sixty, 438 vs 785–882 at eighty — a 50% reduction against the largest. Sharing rises along the same curve and flattens as it saturates — 13%→20%→23%→24% — while multi-witness merges keep accumulating: 24 entries carry three or more witnesses (17 at sixty, nine at forty, three at ten), the deepest still the banquet where Grandmother Jia (贾母) keeps Baoyu (宝玉), Daiyu (黛玉) and Baochai (宝钗) by her side, co-owned by 6. The ordering is the point: the structural properties are architectural and appear immediately, whereas the footprint advantage is a compounding effect that needs enough repeated witnessing to overcome noise. A household world reaches that point later than a war does, because fewer people witness each event.

Merged records in the household world fold family witnesses of one scene:

owners = [jiabaoyu, jiamu, jiazhen, liulaolao, wangxifeng, xuebaochai]  “Grandmother Jia kept only Jia Baoyu, Lin Daiyu and Xue Baochai by her side to receive them.” (贾母只留下贾宝玉、林黛玉与薛宝钗到贾母身边相见。)
owners = [jiahuan, jiazheng, mingyan, pinger, xiren]  “Jia Zheng summoned Jia Baoyu to his study.” (贾政召唤贾宝玉到贾政的书房。)
owners = [jiahuan, jiazheng, pinger, qingwen, xiren]  “Ping’er searched the gallery and the courtyard outside for Jia Baoyu.” (平儿在门廊与院外寻找贾宝玉。)

5.1.4  Hamlet

Discussion. Sixteen agents are enough. Consensus writes 130 entries against 200–214, with 28% shared and 98% linked — the highest sharing rate of any world at any horizon, in the smallest one tested. Run at three horizons, it compounds like the others: sharing goes 19%→26%→28% at twenty, thirty and forty rounds, and three-witness merges appear at thirty (the players’ troupe beginning the performance, owned by the First Player, the Prologue and Guildenstern together) where every merge at twenty had been a strict pair. Depth still lags the larger worlds (2 entries with three or more witnesses, against 38 in Three Kingdoms and 24 in Red Chamber), and the reason is the play’s staging rather than the mechanism’s reach: Shakespeare writes in two-person exchanges — the sentinels on the battlements, Laertes and Polonius, Rosencrantz with Guildenstern — and merge depth tracks how many people the world puts in a room together. The play-within-a-play is the one scene that assembles an audience, and it is exactly where the three-way merges appear.

The pairs the mechanism finds are the play’s own dyads:

owners = [first_player, guildenstern, prologue]  “The troupe of players began the performance of that play at Elsinore.”
owners = [claudius, guildenstern, prologue]  “King Claudius demanded that the play's murder scene be performed exactly and convincingly to draw out Prince Hamlet.”
owners = [guildenstern, rosencrantz]  “At Elsinore, Guildenstern and Rosencrantz decided to watch Hamlet separately.” (在厄耳锡诺城堡，吉尔登斯特恩与罗森克兰茨决定分头监视哈姆雷特。)

5.2  Growth and operation latency

The footprint gap of Table 1 accumulates round by round, and its price is paid at write time. We show both sides for each scenario.

5.2.1  Three Kingdoms (三国演义)

Discussion. The system-level curves separate almost from the start and diverge steadily — the merge saves entries at a roughly constant rate, so its absolute savings compound with horizon rather than saturating; there is no sign of the gap closing by round 80. The per-agent curves show the same mechanism from the individual’s side: growth is stair-stepped (a burst when a character is at the center of a plotline, plateaus when off-stage), and the ranking tracks narrative centrality rather than raw talkativeness — Xu Shu (徐庶) leads because the Xu Shu recruitment arc dominates the middle game, and every merge credits a shared event to all of its witnesses’ curves at once.

Discussion. The two panels show where each design pays. Writes are LLM-bound: every backend pays the shared atomization call, on top of which Generative-Agents adds a per-atom importance call (the most expensive line, 35–75s) and consensus adds the equivalence judge (26–57s), while G-Memory and collaborative write for 10–25s with no per-deposit reasoning beyond atomization. Reads are vector-bound and cheap everywhere (≤1.4s), and — notably — consensus recall is the cheapest of the four (≈0.35s) despite returning ≈28 additional linked memories per call: auto-expansion is plain row lookup, whereas G-Memory’s bi-level retrieval pays for graph traversal with extra vector queries (0.7–1.1s). Neither panel trends upward over 80 rounds: at this scale, store growth (≈7k–22k rows) does not yet move per-call latency, so the consensus premium is a roughly constant per-write tax — the price of P1’s deduplication — paid where agents are least latency-sensitive.

5.2.2  Russia–Ukraine

Discussion. Both figures replay the Three Kingdoms dynamics at a shorter horizon. The system curves separate from round ~3 with consensus lowest and the gap widening, and per-agent growth again concentrates on the situation’s protagonists. The latency ordering of Figure 5 reproduces: writes are LLM-bound (Generative-Agents’ per-atom importance calls most expensive, consensus paying the equivalence-judge tax), while reads are vector-bound and sub-second for all four backends, with consensus recall cheapest despite auto-expansion.

5.2.3  Red Chamber (红楼梦)

Discussion. The domestic world writes more slowly than either other scenario (~5 consensus entries per round against ~20 in Russia–Ukraine) — garden conversation generates fewer memory-worthy events than a war — and the curves that interleaved through the first ten rounds separate cleanly thereafter, consensus lowest and the gap holding to eighty rounds, exactly as in Figures 4 and 6. Per-agent growth concentrates on the household’s centers of gravity (Grandmother Jia 贾母, Wang Xifeng 王熙凤, Jia Baoyu 贾宝玉 and the banquet guests). The read side reproduces both other worlds: consensus recall is cheapest despite auto-expansion returning ≈38 linked memories per call, while G-Memory’s bi-level retrieval pays for graph traversal with extra vector queries.

5.2.4  Hamlet

Discussion. The smallest world writes at a rate between the other two fictions (~3 consensus entries per round), and the four curves separate early with consensus lowest — at this cast size a single merge is a large fraction of a round's writes, so the gap opens without the compounding Red Chamber needed. Latency is dominated by per-call LLM cost exactly as elsewhere; with only 3 recalls over the whole run the read-side curves are too sparse to rank backends, and we read nothing into their ordering here.

5.3  Continuation quality

Every world is judged the same way. Three of the four metrics are read from the run’s rendered screenplay rather than its raw event log (§A.6 prints all four screenplays). The screenplay is the run’s own events dramatized under a no-invention constraint, which buys two things the raw log cannot give: one language per world, whatever the agents happened to emit, and a text an order of magnitude smaller than the transcript, so the judge reads a coherent whole instead of a sampled fragment. Each metric is scored three times and reported mean±1 std:

  • grounding — fraction of the run’s own events consistent with the world’s canon.
  • trajectory — agreement of ten principals’ arcs with arcs extracted from a held-out span: Three Kingdoms chapters 41–60, Red Chamber chapters 41–80, Russia–Ukraine the timeline from 2024-05, Hamlet Acts 4–5.
  • narrative — coherence / distinctiveness / drama / fidelity, 1–5.
  • goal pursuit — of the actions a principal took, the fraction that plausibly serve a goal that was on its own goal stack at that moment. This one is read from the event log, not the screenplay, because goal management is internal: pushing a goal is not a dramatizable beat and never reaches the script. Pursuit is scored, not achievement — an agent that works doggedly at a goal it never reaches should score high, since a faithful tragedy requires goals to fail.

No backend wins this. Of the sixteen world-metric cells, consensus is the best-scoring backend in four of sixteen — narrative in Three Kingdoms; trajectory in Russia-Ukraine and Hamlet; goal pursuit in Russia-Ukraine — and trails the leader in the rest by 0.01–0.06 on the 0–1 metrics and 0.17–0.42 on the 1–5 narrative scale. Those margins are of the same order as the spread across three scorings of the same text. We report this as a wash rather than as a win: compression neither buys judged quality nor costs it, and the case for consensus is made by the structural results of §5.1, not here.

Goal pursuit saturates. All sixteen cells land between 0.96 and 0.99: whatever memory sits underneath, agents do the things they said they were going to do. The reason is structural rather than flattering — the goal stack is part of every agent’s prompt and the kernel prompts an agent with an empty stack to push a goal before acting, so across all four worlds only 0.5–1.6% of actions are taken with no goal held at all. The metric therefore certifies that the agent loop works and separates nothing; we report it because a memory mechanism could have broken it — an agent that cannot recall what it was doing drifts off its own goals — and none of the four does.

5.3.2  Russia–Ukraine

5.3.3  Red Chamber (红楼梦)

5.3.4  Hamlet

Discussion. Three things are worth separating. First, the metrics that should be insensitive to memory architecture are: grounding sits in a narrow band in every world (0.88–0.93 in Three Kingdoms, 0.94–0.97 in Russia–Ukraine) because it is mostly a property of the persona and canon material every backend shares. Second, where consensus does lead it leads on consistency over time — narrative in Three Kingdoms; trajectory in Russia-Ukraine and Hamlet; goal pursuit in Russia-Ukraine — which is what one witness-merged record per event should buy: agents act on the same premises rather than on N drifting paraphrases. Third, and against us, Red Chamber reverses this cleanly: collaborative leads every screenplay metric there, and consensus’s narrative in Russia–Ukraine is last. We do not have a mechanism-level account of either, and with three scorings per cell we do not claim one; the honest reading is that quality differences at this scale are noise around a common mean, while the structural differences of Figure 3 are order-of-magnitude and deterministic. The design argument for consensus rests on structure and footprint, not on these bars.

One scoring caveat, since it bit us: a scoring repeat whose event extraction comes back empty is a harness failure, not a score of zero. Such repeats are retried and, if still empty, dropped from the mean rather than averaged in — an earlier pass reported a spurious 0.59±0.42 for one cell on the strength of a single empty extraction.

5.4  Case study: three graphs over each world

Each world’s consensus run induces the same three graphs: the interaction graph (who talks to whom), the affiliation graph (which memories are linked), and the ownership relation (who owns which memories). For each scenario we show the three layers, then all three in one view, then quantify their pairwise alignment.

5.4.1  Three Kingdoms (三国演义)

The three layers — interactive: drag to pan, scroll to zoom, hover for details, drag nodes to rearrange
All three layers in one view
Pairwise alignment of the layers

A↔O Agents who talk own overlapping memories (0.066 vs 0.003, 23×)

Owned-memory-set Jaccard between agent pairs: the 51 talking pairs average 0.066; the 984 non-talking pairs average 0.003. The entire upper tail belongs to talking pairs.

M↔O Linked memories have the same witnesses (0.77 vs 0.04)

Owner-set Jaccard between memory pairs: the 5640 affiliated pairs mass near 1.0 (mean 0.77); unlinked pairs mass at zero (mean 0.04). One event’s pieces belong to one event’s witnesses.

A↔M Cross-agent memory links follow conversations (116.7 vs 0.07 edges)

Affiliated edges running between two agents’ memory sets: talking pairs average 116.7; non-talking pairs 0.07. The memory graph bridges exactly the agents the conversation graph connects.

Synthesis. The three alignments are not three separate facts but one: the consensus mechanisms transcribe the story’s social structure into the memory substrate. Conversations are where shared experience happens, so merges (ownership overlap) land on talking pairs; deposits narrate the conversation an agent just had, so affiliation clusters coincide with events and their witnesses; and cross-agent links therefore run along conversation edges. In a per-agent store all three relations are identically zero — the substrate cannot express them — which is why the case study is run on the consensus backend alone.

Still the weakest separation of the four worlds, and for a structural reason: a single castle with sixteen residents has few genuinely non-interacting pairs, so the “without” baseline is contaminated by people who simply have not spoken yet — though ten more rounds widened it from 5× to 13× as those pairs met.

5.5  Structure compounds with horizon

Shared and linked structure is not a transient: across the 20/40/60-round checkpoints, sim memories grow roughly linearly while shared memories and affiliated edges grow with them — the merge finds more cross-witness events as the story densifies.

5.5.1  Three Kingdoms (三国演义)

5.5.2  Russia–Ukraine

Forty rounds in a second, structurally different world (real entities, institutional actors, English-language events, a live timeline rather than a novel) reproduce every qualitative claim of §5: fewest entries, exclusive sharing and linking, the three-layer alignment, and the latency profile. The horizon effect predicted by Three Kingdoms is directly observable here: the sharing rate rose 6%→9%→14% at rounds 10/20/40, three-plus-witness merges went from zero to 23, and the deepest merge grew from two witnesses to 10 — a presidential air-defense directive whose single record is co-owned by the president, his chief of staff and adviser, the interior minister, the air-force and intelligence commanders, and the security service — tracking Three Kingdoms’s 19% at 80 rounds on the same compounding curve.

5.6  Agents do not manage memory — mechanisms must

Across all four backends and both models tested, agents issued zero calls to every discretionary memory-management action — linking (add/set/remove_affiliated), explicit link-reading (get_affiliated), forgetting, and revision — despite documentation, worked skill examples, and the id-free query interface. In contrast, the two mechanism-embedded operations carried everything: remember (with atomization, merging, auto-affiliation inside) and recall (with auto-expansion inside; 51/51 recalls returned linked context). We take this as a design principle for agent memory systems: structure must be a side-effect of the operations agents already perform, not a task delegated to them.

5.7  Ablation: which knob does the work

Everything above compares consensus against other designs. This section takes consensus apart. Four cells, one factor at a time from the configuration the paper reports (merge on, FIFO short-term cache), all run on Three Kingdoms (三国演义) for 40 rounds from the same sedimented start under the same code, so only the knob differs. The published run is rerun here rather than reused: the reported run predates the content-language directive of §A.4, and comparing against it would mix a knob with a prompt change. That rerun also serves as a replication — it lands within 1% of the published numbers (6,590 entries against 6,551, sharing 84% against 84%), which is worth knowing given that every number in this paper comes from a single stochastic run.

Table 3. One factor at a time from the published configuration. Structure is deterministic, read from each run’s own export under the same simulation-only accounting as Table 1. The four quality metrics are LLM-judged, mean±1 std over 3 scorings, and all four read the event log rather than a rendered screenplay: rendering would put a separate LLM pass between each cell and its score, which an ablation would then read as mechanism. They therefore compare across cells, not against Table 2.
mergecachewhole storesim entriessharedlinkeddeepestgroundingtrajectorynarrativegoal
onfifo (as published)6,59053919%93%40.92±0.030.89±0.014.17±0.120.97±0.00
onrelevance6,67462321%96%50.93±0.020.83±0.014.33±0.120.99±0.00

offfifo20,6698130%94%10.92±0.020.82±0.024.00±0.000.96±0.00

The merge is doing the work. Disabling it multiplies the store by 3.1× (20,669 entries against 6,590), and the multiplication is concentrated in the sedimented history — 3.3× there against 1.51× for what the simulation itself writes — because a novel deposits one canonical event once per witness. This is the redundancy of P1 measured against its own control rather than against a different system: the same events, the same atomizer, the same agents, with only the equivalence test removed. Sharing goes to exactly zero and the deepest record falls from 4 owners to one.

Sharing and linking are separable, and we had been treating them as one thing. With the merge off, sharing is 0% but linking is 94% — statistically the same as the 93% of the published configuration. The two structures come from different mechanisms: sharing from the equivalence merge, linking from the atomizer, which mutually affiliates the pieces of one compound deposit whether or not anything is ever merged. A system that wanted the memory graph without the compression could have it, and §5.4’s three-layer alignment rests on the linking half, which the merge does not create.

The short-term cache policy is not a research variable. Relevance- and hybrid-based eviction leave every structural quantity where FIFO leaves it (sharing 18–21%, linking 96%), while costing 15–19% more wall-clock, since each cached line must be embedded to be scored. They do write 84–80 more entries, but that is agents holding different context and therefore saying different things, not a property of the memory mechanism. FIFO is reported as the default because nothing recommends the alternatives, not because they were tuned away.

None of the four quality metrics separates on the merge. Grounding lands at 0.92, 0.93, 0.94 and 0.92 across the four cells — a band narrower than one cell’s own scoring spread — and goal pursuit is flat at 0.96–0.99, as it is everywhere else in this paper. Narrative is the widest spread (4.00 with the merge off against 4.33 for relevance eviction) and trajectory the only one that orders the cells the way the mechanism would predict (0.89 and 0.90 with the merge on against 0.82 without it), which is what agents acting on one merged record rather than several drifting copies should buy — but at three scorings per cell we report it as suggestive, not as an effect. An earlier version of this ablation scored grounding from a transcript that carried only speech, and produced a spread that looked like a merge penalty; feeding the judge every logged action instead removed it. What the merge changes is the store, not the story.

6 Discussion and Limitations

What consensus buys. Under equal granularity and sim-only accounting, consensus dominates structurally — fewest entries, all sharing, all graph structure — and buys this at no measurable cost in judged quality: across four worlds and three metrics the four backends land within noise of one another, with no backend leading everywhere and consensus leading three cells of twelve (§5.3). The three-layer alignment argues the structure is meaningful: it recovers the story’s social organization from the memory substrate alone.

Limitations. (i) Quality metrics are LLM-judged and noisy; we report 3-scoring means with std, but ranking claims beyond narrative should be treated cautiously. (ii) Results cover one scenario (Three Kingdoms) and one 60-round horizon; the protocol ports directly to other sedimented worlds and longer runs (checkpoints exist), but those runs remain future work. (iii) Auto-expansion is deliberately uncapped, appending ≈28 linked memories per recall; this enriches context but grows prompts, and its cost–benefit curve is unmeasured. (iv) The equivalence judge and atomizer consume extra LLM calls per deposit — the price of compression is paid at write time. (v) One baseline artifact: G-Memory re-runs distillation on resume (its distill bookkeeping is not check-pointed); sim-only accounting excludes distillation nodes, so reported numbers are unaffected.

7 Conclusion

Agentsensus treats a story world’s memory as a single consensus store: equivalent memories merge across witnesses, split memories link into a graph, and recall walks that graph automatically. On a novel-seeded 80-round simulation, this yields the smallest memory footprint at equal granularity, the only shared and linked memory structure among four backends, and an emergent memory graph that mirrors the story’s social structure — while judged continuation quality stays within noise of the baselines in all four worlds. The broader lesson is that memory structure in multi-agent systems must be mechanized, not delegated: agents reliably use only remember and recall, so that is where the structure has to live.

A Appendix

The appendix reports material the main text summarizes or omits: a census of what agents actually do with the action repertoire (A.1), transcript excerpts from all four worlds with a reading of how each memory design shows up in behavior (A.2), the sedimentation and cast-selection numbers behind each world (A.3), the language composition of the runs (A.4), and the merge-depth and expansion statistics behind the structural claims (A.5).

A.1  What agents actually call

§5.6 asserts that agents never perform memory management. Table A1 is the evidence in full: every action invocation across the four worlds’ final stages, by backend. The repertoire is identical for all four and documented in the same skill file, with worked examples; the id-free query addressing of §3.7 removes the interface barrier that an earlier design was suspected of having.

Reading. The memory interface agents actually use is two calls wide. remember runs 8–84 times per backend per world and recall 0–12, and every one of the six discretionary memory-management actions sits at zero in every world — the empirical basis for D3, since a mechanism placed behind add_affiliated would simply never run. Two further readings. The distribution is nearly identical across backends within a world, which is what the fairness protocol wants: the backends differ in what remember and recall do, not in how often they are called. And writes outnumber reads by roughly 8:1 in the novels and 15:1 in Russia–Ukraine — agents deposit far more than they retrieve, which is why §5.2 treats the write path as the one whose cost matters. Hamlet is the sharpest case: recall was invoked zero times by any backend across 40 rounds, so its whole run is written memory that no agent ever asked for again.

A.2  Transcript excerpts

One deduplicated say message per backend, from each world’s final stage, chosen by length so a block fits here; only the recipient list is abridged. The two Chinese worlds are given in English with the original beneath; the two English worlds are given as written. The point of the comparison is not prose quality — §5.3 measures that and finds the backends within error bars of one another — but what a memory design looks like from the outside.

Russia–Ukraine (40 rounds, English)

consensus  [r24] un → guterres
“Rosemary DiCarlo, please begin your 5-minute brief now and name the DPA drafting lead for the Security Council text.”
generative-agents  [r24] iaea → grossi

These are English-language excerpts, but not every message in this world was English: 12% of the run’s memories are Chinese and 2% Russian (Table A3), the latter because agents adopted the language of the character they were playing.

Hamlet (40 rounds, English)

consensus  [r24] fortinbras → marcellus
“Marcellus, report the current troop and weapon counts on the battlements, and prepare to escort me to the Great Hall so we can inventory arms and gather grain.”
generative-agents  [r20] marcellus → barnardo
“Barnardo — go wake Horatio at once and tell him to come to the battlements immediately. Do not go alone; wait here until he arrives.”
g-memory  [r28] barnardo → horatio
“Horatio, Marcellus and I just saw a ghost on the battlements.”
collaborative  [r20] first_player → rosencrantz
“Thank you, Rosencrantz. I’m glad the play is engaging. Watch King Claudius closely and tell me if his countenance changes during the performance.”

Reading. Three things hold across all four worlds. The register is set by the action repertoire, not by the memory design. Every backend drifts toward administrative correspondence — requests, confirmations, rosters, timings — because what an agent can do is speak, set goals, and report; Red Chamber’s poetry club and Hamlet’s battlements are pulled into the same idiom as Three Kingdoms’s supply trains. The worlds differ more than the backends do. The institutional worlds produce long procedural messages (Russia–Ukraine’s shortest English line runs 285 characters); the chamber drama produces short ones (“Horatio, Marcellus and I just saw a ghost on the battlements”); the household world sits between, with etiquette carrying most of the content.

What does track the memory design is the direction of reference. Consensus lines characteristically ask which branch of an already-shared arrangement now applies — Cheng Yu (程昱) asks whether the pickup still stands at midnight or has moved to the post-house; Baoyu (宝玉) asks whether to sit now or wait for Daiyu (黛玉); the UN chair asks a named official to begin the brief. The speaker treats the prior arrangement as a record both sides hold and asks only for the delta. Baseline lines more often re-establish the arrangement before acting on it: Mi Zhu (糜竺) restates troop count, rations, and the sealing of the granary; Xu Chu (许褚) re-reports the whole scouting result; Jia Lian (贾琏) asks for names, business, and proof of identity that the household already has. That is what an agent does when it cannot assume the other party’s copy matches its own. The pattern is consistent with the mechanism — N witnesses holding one row do not need to re-establish premises — but it is an observation on selected excerpts, not a measurement; the quality metrics of §5.3 put the backends within each other’s error bars, and we do not claim more than that.

One artifact worth recording, because it affects anything built on the event log: the kernel logs a single utterance both as an action event and as one message event per recipient, so a line addressed to three agents appears four times. Naive transcript assembly therefore triples parts of a run; the excerpts above and the screenplay renderer both deduplicate by (round, speaker, content).

A.3  Sedimentation and cast selection

Each world is built by the pipeline of §3.4 and then reduced to a simulable cast. A character participates iff it owns more than a per-world threshold of sediment memories; below-threshold characters remain owners of their memories but are never scheduled. Environments are kept if an active character stands there or if they own memories of their own; information carriers (letters, commissions, play scripts) are always kept.

Table A2. Sedimentation cost and cast composition. Wall-clock and token figures are for the sedimentation pass only, on the consensus store; the per-backend ingest of the same events is additional. “Warnings” counts extraction records the pipeline flagged for review (unresolved referents, ambiguous attributions).

Reading. Cost tracks source length, not cast size: Russia–Ukraine extracts the fewest events (1,533 dated entries) yet costs the most tokens, because a timeline entry names many institutional actors and attribution must resolve each one. The archived column is the boundary-state finalization of §3.4 at work and is worth reading per world: Three Kingdoms archives 38 characters dead by chapter 40; Red Chamber archives three (秦可卿, 贾瑞, 秦钟); Hamlet archives Polonius, killed in 3.4, and the Ghost, absent from the canon thereafter; Russia–Ukraine archives 14 under real-world semantics, where “no longer a participant” covers leaving office or being disbanded as well as dying, and where every placement was verified by hand against the 2026-07 boundary. Two cases required overrides that no automatic rule would produce: Fortinbras owns zero sediment memories — he never appears before Act 4 — but is retained because the continuation is his, and England is retained as an environment for the same reason.

A.4  Language composition of the runs

Each world declares a language: Three Kingdoms and Red Chamber run in Chinese, Russia–Ukraine and Hamlet in English. The declaration selects the action-skill document and the output-format block, and the sediment is in the source language throughout. It did not, in the runs reported here, constrain what agents wrote: the language of a memory followed the language of the profile and of whatever the agent recalled, and drifted when those disagreed.

Table A3. Language of simulation memories (consensus store, final stage of each world). Classification is by script: an entry with CJK characters and no substantial Latin text counts as Chinese, an entry with both counts as mixed, Cyrillic-dominant entries count as Russian.
worlddeclaredChineseEnglishmixedRussian
Three Kingdoms (三国演义)zh90%9%——
Red Chamber (红楼梦)zh97%1%1%—
Russia–Ukraineen12%81%2%2%
Hamleten26%59%14%—

Reading. The drift is largest where the two implicit signals disagree most. All four worlds carried Chinese-authored character profiles, so an English world with an English sediment still pulled toward Chinese, and Hamlet — the smallest sediment, hence the weakest counterweight — drifted furthest (26% Chinese, 14% mixed). Russia–Ukraine additionally produced Russian-language memories: agents adopted the language of the character they were playing, which no instruction had asked for and none had forbidden. We report this as a finding about implicit conditioning rather than a defect of the memory mechanisms, which are language-agnostic: entry counts, sharing, and graph structure are unaffected. The framework now carries an explicit content-language directive in the agent system prompt, and screenplays are normalized to the world’s language at render time; the runs above predate the directive and were not regenerated for it.

A.5  Merge depth, graph density, and expansion

§5.1 reports the share of memories that are shared and linked. The distribution behind those shares, and what recall does with the graph, are below.

Table A4. Consensus structure per world (final stage). “3+” counts entries with three or more witnesses; “max” is the deepest merge; “expanded” is the fraction of recalls that returned at least one memory reached along an affiliated edge, with the mean number of such memories per call.

Russia–Ukraine (40t)814113 (14%)231099%23/412
Hamlet (40t)11029 (26%)1398%3/339

Reading. Merge depth is a property of the world’s staging, not of the mechanism. Russia–Ukraine reaches ten witnesses on a single presidential air-defense directive because a real command chain broadcasts one instruction to many named institutions at once; Hamlet tops out at three, and only once — on the players’ performance, the one scene in the play that assembles an audience — because Shakespeare stages almost everything as a two-person exchange. The two novels sit between, at six. Expansion behaves differently for a different reason: it returns few linked memories in Russia–Ukraine (2 per call, and only 23 of 41 recalls expanded at all) because institutional deposits are short and rarely split into several atoms, so there are fewer siblings to link; in the novels a single compound recollection atomizes into many pieces, and a recall pulls back 28–39 of them. The sharing rate itself is horizon-dependent and saturating — Red Chamber, run at four horizons, goes 13%→20%→23%→24% at rounds 10/40/60/80 — which is the compounding argument of §5.1.3 measured directly.

A.6  Screenplays

The full screenplay of each world’s consensus run, rendered from its event log by the pipeline of §5.3: beats are grouped into scenes by place and stretch of time, each scene is dramatized in one grounded pass, and a check-and-repair round catches any beat the renderer dropped. Nothing outside the log may appear — the cast, the location and every action are constrained to what the run actually produced — while the wording must be rewritten rather than copied, with no line running longer than a spoken breath and no memo formatting inside dialogue. This is the text the continuation-quality judge reads.

Each screenplay is long — between twelve and sixty-two scenes — so the four are collapsed by default and printed after the grids below.

Table A5. The four screenplays. “Beats” are the dramatizable events the run produced after deduplication (one utterance is one beat, however many recipients it was logged against); “scenes” are the groupings of those beats by place and stretch of time that each become one render call. Length is the rendered markdown; the Chinese worlds carry two renderings of the same beats.
worldroundsscenesbeatsspeakersplacesEnglishsource language
Three Kingdoms 三国演义0–79543123324206k chars62k chars (zh)
Red Chamber 红楼梦0–7962390342698k chars30k chars (zh)
Russia–Ukraine0–39483344720313k chars— (en)
Hamlet0–391211716649k chars— (en)

Reading. Scene count tracks how scattered a world is, not how much happens in it: Hamlet’s 117 beats fall into 12 scenes because the play keeps returning to the same six places, while Red Chamber’s 390 beats spread over 26 locations and split into 62. Length per beat is a property of what the agents say, not of how many of them speak: Russia–Ukraine writes 313k characters from 334 beats because an institutional order carries a page of particulars the renderer may not drop, while Red Chamber’s 390 beats come to 30k characters in Chinese because a household exchange is mostly short questions. The English rendering of a Chinese world runs about three times the length of its source-language twin, which is a property of the writing systems rather than of the content.

A note on register: the dialogue reads administratively because the simulation does. Agents can speak, set goals and report, so they write like officers filing returns; the screenplay can stage that exchange, give it voices and cut it into speakable lines, but it cannot make a supply conference lyrical. §A.2 makes the same point from the raw transcripts.

How the scenes were cut. One figure per world: every cell is one round at one place, coloured when an agent acted there. The four are read the same way, so the first is annotated in full and the rest carry only what is particular to that world.

The screenplays themselves follow, one collapsible block per world, in the same order. The Chinese worlds are given in English with the scenario-language rendering beneath each scene; both are produced directly from the same beats in a single pass, not by translating one into the other.
